units.en: Euryclea now went upstairs laughing to tell her mistress that her dear husband had come home. Her aged knees became young again and her feet were nimble for joy as she went up to her mistress and bent over her head to speak to her. “Wake up Penelope, my dear child,” she exclaimed, “and see with your own eyes something that you have been wanting this long time past. Ulysses has at last indeed come home again, and has killed the suitors who were giving so much trouble in his house, eating up his estate and ill treating his son.”
units.ja: エウリュクレイアは笑いながら二階へ上がり、女主人のもとへ行って、愛する夫が帰ってきたことを知らせた。老いた膝は若返ったように軽やかで、喜びのあまり足どりも速かった。彼女は女主人のもとへ行き、その頭の上に身をかがめて話しかけた。「目をお覚ましください、ペネロペ、かわいい子や」と彼女は叫んだ。「あなたが長いあいだずっと待ち望んでいらしたものを、この目でごらんになるのです。オデュッセウスがとうとう本当に帰ってきました。そして、この家でさんざん面倒をかけ、財産を食いつぶし、息子さんをひどく扱っていた求婚者たちを、殺してしまったのです。」

notes.title: エウリュクレイア
notes.body: オデュッセウスの家に仕える老いた乳母。幼いオデュッセウスを育てた人物で、家の内情に詳しく、主人に忠実なことで知られる。
notes.bodyEn: The old nurse who serves Odysseus's household. She raised Odysseus as a child, is well acquainted with the household's inner affairs, and is known for her loyalty to her master.

units.en: “My good nurse,” answered Penelope, “you must be mad. The gods sometimes send some very sensible people out of their minds, and make foolish people become sensible. This is what they must have been doing to you; for you always used to be a reasonable person. Why should you thus mock me when I have trouble enough already—talking such nonsense, and waking me up out of a sweet sleep that had taken possession of my eyes and closed them? I have never slept so soundly from the day my poor husband went to that city with the ill-omened name. Go back again into the women’s room; if it had been any one else who had woke me up to bring me such absurd news I should have sent her away with a severe scolding. As it is your age shall protect you.”
units.ja: 「まあ、よくしてくれる乳母よ」とペネロペは答えた。「あなたは気がふれているにちがいありません。神々はときに、たいそう分別のある人を正気から遠ざけ、愚かな者を分別のある者に変えてしまうことがあります。あなたにもきっとそれと同じことが起きているのでしょう。あなたはいつも分別のある人でしたから。もう十分すぎるほどの苦労を抱えているこの私を、どうしてそんなふうにからかうのですか。そんなたわごとを言い、私のまぶたをとらえて閉じさせていた心地よい眠りから私を起こすなんて。女部屋へお帰りなさい。もし他の誰かが、こんな馬鹿げた知らせを持ってきて私を起こしたのなら、きつく叱って追い払っていたところです。ですが今は、あなたの年齢があなたを守ってくれます。」

notes.title: 忌まわしい名の町
notes.body: トロイアを指す。夫がそこへ発った日からペネロペは長く苦しんできたため、その町の名を口にするのさえ忌まわしく感じている。原文でも町の名そのものに不吉な響きが込められている。
notes.titleEn: The town of the hateful name
notes.bodyEn: This refers to Troy. Because Penelope has suffered long since the day her husband set out for it, she finds even speaking the town's name hateful. In the original, too, the town's very name carries an ominous ring.

units.en: “My dear child,” answered Euryclea, “I am not mocking you. It is quite true as I tell you that Ulysses is come home again. He was the stranger whom they all kept on treating so badly in the cloister. Telemachus knew all the time that he was come back, but kept his father’s secret that he might have his revenge on all these wicked people.”
units.ja: 「かわいい子や」とエウリュクレイアは答えた。「からかってなどおりません。オデュッセウスが帰ってきたと申し上げたのは、まったく本当のことです。あの方は、中庭で皆がさんざんひどい扱いをしていた、あの旅の人でした。テレマコスは、父が戻っていることをずっと知っていましたが、あの悪者どもに復讐するために、父の秘密を守っていたのです。」

notes.title: テレマコス
notes.body: オデュッセウスとペネロペの息子。父の帰還を早くから知りながら、求婚者たちへの復讐のためにそれを隠していた。
notes.bodyEn: The son of Odysseus and Penelope. Although he knew of his father's return from early on, he concealed it in order to take revenge on the suitors.

units.en: Then Penelope sprang up from her couch, threw her arms round Euryclea, and wept for joy. “But my dear nurse,” said she, “explain this to me; if he has really come home as you say, how did he manage to overcome the wicked suitors single handed, seeing what a number of them there always were?”
units.ja: そこでペネロペは寝床から跳び起き、エウリュクレイアに両腕を回して抱きつき、うれしさのあまり泣いた。「でも乳母よ」と彼女は言った。「これを説明してください。もしあなたの言うとおり本当に帰ってきたのなら、いつもあれほど大勢いた悪い求婚者たちを、どうやってたった一人で打ち負かしたのですか。」

units.en: “I was not there,” answered Euryclea, “and do not know; I only heard them groaning while they were being killed. We sat crouching and huddled up in a corner of the women’s room with the doors closed, till your son came to fetch me because his father sent him. Then I found Ulysses standing over the corpses that were lying on the ground all round him, one on top of the other. You would have enjoyed it if you could have seen him standing there all bespattered with blood and filth, and looking just like a lion. But the corpses are now all piled up in the gatehouse that is in the outer court, and Ulysses has lit a great fire to purify the house with sulphur. He has sent me to call you, so come with me that you may both be happy together after all; for now at last the desire of your heart has been fulfilled; your husband is come home to find both wife and son alive and well, and to take his revenge in his own house on the suitors who behaved so badly to him.”
units.ja: 「私はそこにいたのではありません」とエウリュクレイアは答えた。「ですから知りません。ただ、彼らが殺されるときにうめく声だけは聞きました。私たちは女部屋の隅に身を寄せ合ってうずくまり、戸を閉ざしたままでした。やがてあなたの息子が、父に命じられて私を呼びに来ました。それから私は、オデュッセウスが、地面に横たわり幾重にも重なった屍の上に立っているのを見ました。血と汚れにまみれて、まるで獅子のように立っているあの姿を、ごらんになったら、あなたもさぞお喜びになったでしょう。ですが屍は今、外庭にある門の建物にすべて積み上げられています。オデュッセウスは家を硫黄で清めるために、大きな火を焚きました。私を呼びにやったのも、あなたを連れてくるためです。さあ、一緒に参りましょう。そうすれば、これほどのことを経て、お二人とも一緒に幸せになれます。ようやくあなたの心の望みがかないました。夫が帰ってきて、妻も息子も無事で健やかなのを見いだし、自分をひどく扱った求婚者たちに、自分の家で復讐を果たしたのですから。」

notes.title: 硫黄による清め
notes.body: 人を殺した家を再び使えるようにするための浄めの儀式。硫黄を焚いてその煙で穢れを払う作法で、殺害のあった場所を清める意味をもつ。
notes.bodyEn: A rite of purification for making a house where a person has been killed usable again. By burning sulfur and driving out pollution with its smoke, it carries the meaning of cleansing the place where the killing occurred.

units.en: “My dear nurse,” said Penelope, “do not exult too confidently over all this. You know how delighted every one would be to see Ulysses come home—more particularly myself, and the son who has been born to both of us; but what you tell me cannot be really true. It is some god who is angry with the suitors for their great wickedness, and has made an end of them; for they respected no man in the whole world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them, and they have come to a bad end in consequence of their iniquity; Ulysses is dead far away from the Achaean land; he will never return home again.”
units.ja: 「乳母よ」とペネロペは言った。「あまり勝手に喜んではいけません。オデュッセウスが帰ってくるのを見たら誰もがどんなに喜ぶか、あなたも知っているでしょう。とりわけ私、そして二人のあいだに生まれた息子は。ですが、あなたの話は本当ではありえません。求婚者たちのひどい悪行に怒った神がいて、その神が彼らを滅ぼしたのです。彼らは、近づいてくる人を、金持ちでも貧しい者でも、世界中で誰一人として敬いませんでした。その不義のゆえに、彼らは悪い最期を迎えたのです。オデュッセウスはアカイアの地から遠く離れたところで死にました。もう二度と帰ってはきません。」

units.en: Then nurse Euryclea said, “My child, what are you talking about? but you were all hard of belief and have made up your mind that your husband is never coming, although he is in the house and by his own fire side at this very moment. Besides I can give you another proof; when I was washing him I perceived the scar which the wild boar gave him, and I wanted to tell you about it, but in his wisdom he would not let me, and clapped his hands over my mouth; so come with me and I will make this bargain with you—if I am deceiving you, you may have me killed by the most cruel death you can think of.”
units.ja: そこで乳母エウリュクレイアは言った。「わが子よ、何を言うのですか。あなたも皆も信じようとせず、夫はもう帰ってこないと決め込んでしまったのに、その夫は今この瞬間、家の中、自分の炉辺にいるのですよ。それにもう一つ証拠があります。私が彼の体を洗ったとき、猪がつけたあの傷痕に気づきました。あなたに話そうとしたのですが、賢明な彼はそれを許さず、私の口に手を当ててふさぎました。ですから一緒にいらしてください。そしてこう約束しましょう。もし私があなたを欺いているのなら、あなたが思いつくかぎりで最も残酷な死に方を、私にさせてもかまいません。」

notes.title: 猪の傷痕
notes.body: オデュッセウスが若いころ、山で猪に襲われて脚に負った傷。乳母だけが知る、彼を本人と見分けるためのしるしになっている。
notes.bodyEn: A wound Odysseus received on his leg when, in his youth, he was attacked by a boar in the mountains. Known only to his nurse, it serves as the mark by which he is identified as the man himself.

units.en: “My dear nurse,” said Penelope, “however wise you may be you can hardly fathom the counsels of the gods. Nevertheless, we will go in search of my son, that I may see the corpses of the suitors, and the man who has killed them.”
units.ja: 「乳母よ」とペネロペは言った。「あなたがどんなに賢くとも、神々の計らいを推し量ることはとてもできません。それでも、息子のところへ行ってみましょう。求婚者たちの屍と、彼らを殺した男を見るために。」

units.en: On this she came down from her upper room, and while doing so she considered whether she should keep at a distance from her husband and question him, or whether she should at once go up to him and embrace him. When, however, she had crossed the stone floor of the cloister, she sat down opposite Ulysses by the fire, against the wall at right angles [to that by which she had entered], while Ulysses sat near one of the bearing-posts, looking upon the ground, and waiting to see what his brave wife would say to him when she saw him. For a long time she sat silent and as one lost in amazement. At one moment she looked him full in the face, but then again directly, she was misled by his shabby clothes and failed to recognise him, till Telemachus began to reproach her and said:
units.ja: そこで彼女は二階の部屋から降りてきた。その途中、夫から離れたまま問いただそうか、それともすぐに近づいて抱きしめようかと考えた。だが、中庭の石の床を渡り終えると、彼女は、自分が入ってきた壁と直角に交わる壁ぎわで、炉辺のオデュッセウスと向かい合って腰をおろした。オデュッセウスは柱の一本のそばに座り、地面を見つめながら、勇気ある妻が自分を見て何を言うのかと待っていた。長いあいだ、彼女は黙ったまま、驚きに我を忘れたように座っていた。あるときは彼の顔をじっと見つめたが、すぐにまた、みすぼらしい衣服に惑わされて、彼と気づくことができなかった。そこへテレマコスが母を責めはじめ、こう言った。

units.en: “Mother—but you are so hard that I cannot call you by such a name—why do you keep away from my father in this way? Why do you not sit by his side and begin talking to him and asking him questions? No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much; but your heart always was as hard as a stone.”
units.ja: 「母上——ですが、あなたはあまりに心が硬くて、私にはその名で呼ぶことができません——なぜこんなふうに父から離れているのですか。なぜ父のそばに座り、話しかけ、問いただそうとしないのですか。二十年の不在の末に、あれほどの苦難を経て夫が戻ってきたのに、夫から離れたままでいられる女はほかにいません。しかし、あなたの心はいつも石のように硬かったのでした。」

units.en: Penelope answered, “My son, I am so lost in astonishment that I can find no words in which either to ask questions or to answer them. I cannot even look him straight in the face. Still, if he really is Ulysses come back to his own home again, we shall get to understand one another better by and by, for there are tokens with which we two are alone acquainted, and which are hidden from all others.”
units.ja: ペネロペは答えた。「息子よ、私は驚きのあまり我を忘れてしまって、問いを立てる言葉も、それに答える言葉も見つかりません。まっすぐに顔を見ることさえできないのです。それでも、もし本当に彼がオデュッセウスで、自分の家に帰ってきたのなら、やがて私たちはもっとよく分かり合えるでしょう。私たち二人だけが知っていて、他の誰にも隠されているしるしがあるのですから。」

units.en: Ulysses smiled at this, and said to Telemachus, “Let your mother put me to any proof she likes; she will make up her mind about it presently. She rejects me for the moment and believes me to be somebody else, because I am covered with dirt and have such bad clothes on; let us, however, consider what we had better do next. When one man has killed another—even though he was not one who would leave many friends to take up his quarrel—the man who has killed him must still say good bye to his friends and fly the country; whereas we have been killing the stay of a whole town, and all the picked youth of Ithaca. I would have you consider this matter.”
units.ja: オデュッセウスはこれを聞いて微笑み、テレマコスに言った。「母に好きなだけ私を試させるがよい。彼女もじきに決心するだろう。今は私を拒み、他の誰かだと思っているのだ。私が汚れにまみれ、こんなみすぼらしい服を着ているために。だが、次にどうするのがよいか考えよう。人が人を殺したときは——たとえ、その者のために争ってくれる友人が多くない相手であっても——殺した者は友人に別れを告げ、国を逃れねばならない。それなのに、私たちは町全体の支えであり、イタケーの選り抜きの若者たちをすべて殺してしまったのだ。このことをよく考えてほしい。」

notes.title: イタケー
notes.body: オデュッセウスの故郷である島。ここで殺された求婚者たちは、この島の有力な家柄の若者たちだった。
notes.bodyEn: The island that is Odysseus's homeland. The suitors killed here were young men of the island's leading families.

units.en: “Look to it yourself, father,” answered Telemachus, “for they say you are the wisest counsellor in the world, and that there is no other mortal man who can compare with you. We will follow you with right good will, nor shall you find us fail you in so far as our strength holds out.”
units.ja: 「それを決めるのはあなた自身です、父上」とテレマコスは答えた。「あなたは世界中で最も優れた助言者であり、あなたに比べられる人間はほかにいないと、皆が言っていますから。私たちは喜んであなたに従いますし、私たちの力が続くかぎり、あなたを裏切ることはありません。」

units.en: “I will say what I think will be best,” answered Ulysses. “First wash and put your shirts on; tell the maids also to go to their own room and dress; Phemius shall then strike up a dance tune on his lyre, so that if people outside hear, or any of the neighbours, or some one going along the street happens to notice it, they may think there is a wedding in the house, and no rumours about the death of the suitors will get about in the town, before we can escape to the woods upon my own land. Once there, we will settle which of the courses heaven vouchsafes us shall seem wisest.”
units.ja: 「私が最善と思うことを言おう」とオデュッセウスは答えた。「まず体を洗い、上衣を着なさい。女中たちにも自分の部屋へ行って支度をするように言いなさい。それからフェミオスに竪琴で舞の曲を奏でさせなさい。外にいる者や隣人たち、あるいは通りがかりの誰かがそれを耳にして、この家で婚礼があるのだと思い、私が自分の領地の森へ逃れる前に、求婚者たちの死の噂が町に広まらないようにするためだ。森に着いたら、天がわれわれに与えてくれる道のうち、どれが最も賢明と思われるかを決めよう。」

notes.title: フェミオス
notes.body: イタケーで歌をうたう吟遊詩人。この家の広間で求婚者たちに歌を聞かせていたが、殺害の難は免れている。
notes.bodyEn: The bard who sings songs in Ithaca. He had been performing songs for the suitors in the hall of this house, but he escapes the calamity of slaughter.

units.en: Thus did he speak, and they did even as he had said. First they washed and put their shirts on, while the women got ready. Then Phemius took his lyre and set them all longing for sweet song and stately dance. The house re-echoed with the sound of men and women dancing, and the people outside said, “I suppose the queen has been getting married at last. She ought to be ashamed of herself for not continuing to protect her husband’s property until he comes home.”
units.ja: こう彼が言うと、一同はそのとおりにした。まず男たちは身を洗って肌着をまとい、女たちは支度を整えた。次いでフェミオスが竪琴を手に取り、甘い歌とおごそかな舞踏へのあこがれを皆の胸に呼び起こした。館は男たち女たちの踊る音をこだまのように響かせ、外にいた人々は言った。「どうやら王妃はとうとう結婚したらしい。夫の財産を、夫が帰ってくるまで守り続けるのをやめたとは、自分でも恥ずかしいと思っているだろうに。」

notes.title: フェミオス
notes.body: イタケの館に仕える吟遊詩人。膳部の宴の席で歌をうたい、この場面でも舞踏の音頭を取る役を担う。
notes.bodyEn: The bard who serves the house in Ithaca. He sings at the feast in the hall, and in this scene too he takes on the role of leading the dance.

units.en: This was what they said, but they did not know what it was that had been happening. The upper servant Eurynome washed and anointed Ulysses in his own house and gave him a shirt and cloak, while Minerva made him look taller and stronger than before; she also made the hair grow thick on the top of his head, and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms; she glorified him about the head and shoulders just as a skilful workman who has studied art of all kinds under Vulcan or Minerva—and his work is full of beauty—enriches a piece of silver plate by gilding it. He came from the bath looking like one of the immortals, and sat down opposite his wife on the seat he had left. “My dear,” said he, “heaven has endowed you with a heart more unyielding than woman ever yet had. No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he had come back to her after twenty years of absence, and after having gone through so much. But come, nurse, get a bed ready for me; I will sleep alone, for this woman has a heart as hard as iron.”
units.ja: 人々はそう言ったが、実際に何が起こっていたのかは知らなかった。侍女頭のエウリュノメが、オデュッセウスを彼自身の館で洗い、油を塗り、肌着と外套を与えた。そのあいだアテナは、彼を以前よりも背を高く、たくましく見せ、また頭の髪を房厚く生やして、ヒュアキントスの花のような巻き毛にして流れさせた。女神は彼の頭と肩を、あたかも、ヘパイストスやアテナのもとであらゆる技を学んだ巧みな工人が、その仕事に美しさを満ちあふれさせて、銀の器を金でめっきして飾り立てるように、輝かせた。彼は浴場から不死の神々の一人のような姿で現れ、自分がさきほどまで座っていた席に、妻と向かい合って腰を下ろした。「妻よ」と彼は言った。「天はお前に、これまでどの女も持たなかったほど頑なな心を与えたようだ。二十年の不在のすえ、これほどの苦難を経て夫が戻ってきても、ほかの女なら、夫から離れていることなど耐えられない。だが、乳母よ、私の寝床を整えてくれ。私は一人で寝るつもりだ。この女の心は鉄のように固いからな。」

notes.title: ウルカヌス（ヘパイストス）
notes.body: 原文の Vulcan はローマ神話の鍛冶の神で、ギリシア神話のヘパイストスにあたる。本訳ではギリシア名に統一した。
notes.bodyEn: Vulcan in the original is the Roman god of the forge, corresponding to Hephaestus in Greek myth. This translation standardizes it to the Greek name.

units.en: “My dear,” answered Penelope, “I have no wish to set myself up, nor to depreciate you; but I am not struck by your appearance, for I very well remember what kind of a man you were when you set sail from Ithaca. Nevertheless, Euryclea, take his bed outside the bed chamber that he himself built. Bring the bed outside this room, and put bedding upon it with fleeces, good coverlets, and blankets.”
units.ja: 「旦那さま」とペネロペは答えた。「私は自分を高く見せたいとも、あなたを貶めたいとも思いません。ただ、あなたの姿を見ても、それと分からないのです。イタケを船出されたとき、あなたがどんな人だったかは、よく覚えておりますから。けれどエウリュクレイア、あの人が自分で作った寝台を寝室の外へ運び出しておくれ。この部屋から寝台を外へ出し、羊の毛皮と上等な掛け布と毛布を敷いてやっておくれ。」

notes.title: エウリュクレイア
notes.body: オデュッセウスを幼い頃から育てた乳母で、館の女たちを取り仕切る立場にある。前段で「乳母よ」と呼びかけられた相手でもある。
notes.bodyEn: The nurse who raised Odysseus from infancy and holds the position of directing the women of the house. She is also the one addressed as "nurse" in the preceding passage.

units.en: She said this to try him, but Ulysses was very angry and said, “Wife, I am much displeased at what you have just been saying. Who has been taking my bed from the place in which I left it? He must have found it a hard task, no matter how skilled a workman he was, unless some god came and helped him to shift it. There is no man living, however strong and in his prime, who could move it from its place, for it is a marvellous curiosity which I made with my very own hands. There was a young olive growing within the precincts of the house, in full vigour, and about as thick as a bearing-post. I built my room round this with strong walls of stone and a roof to cover them, and I made the doors strong and well-fitting. Then I cut off the top boughs of the olive tree and left the stump standing. This I dressed roughly from the root upwards and then worked with carpenter’s tools well and skilfully, straightening my work by drawing a line on the wood, and making it into a bed-prop. I then bored a hole down the middle, and made it the centre-post of my bed, at which I worked till I had finished it, inlaying it with gold and silver; after this I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side of it to the other. So you see I know all about it, and I desire to learn whether it is still there, or whether any one has been removing it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots.”
units.ja: ペネロペは彼を試すためにそう言ったのだが、オデュッセウスはひどく怒って言った。「妻よ、今のお前の言葉には、まったく心穏やかでいられない。誰が私の寝台を、私が置いた場所から動かしたのだ。どんなに腕のよい工人であれ、神が手を貸して動かすのでなければ、それは難儀な仕事だったはずだ。どれほど強く、壮年の男であろうと、これを元の場所から動かせる者は、今の世に一人もいない。これは私がこの両手で作った、不思議な逸品なのだから。かつて家の敷地の中に、勢いよく育った若いオリーブが、ちょうど梁受けの柱ほどの太さで生えていた。その周りに私は石の頑丈な壁を巡らし、それをおおう屋根を架け、扉も丈夫に、ぴったりと合わせて作った。そしてオリーブの上の枝を切り落とし、株はそのまま立たせておいた。これを根のあたりから上へ粗削りに整え、さらに大工の道具で巧みに仕上げ、木に線を引いて仕事をまっすぐにしながら、寝台の支柱に作り変えた。それから真ん中へ縦に穴をあけ、寝台の中心の柱とした。それを私は金と銀をちりばめて作り上げ、そのうえで片側からもう片側へ、深紅の革を張り渡した。これだけのことを私は知っている。そこで、あれが今もそこにあるのか、それとも誰かがオリーブを根もとから切り倒して片づけてしまったのか、知りたいのだ。」

notes.title: オリーブの寝台
notes.body: 切り株をそのまま支柱に据えた寝台。根を断たずに部屋を建てているため、元の場所から動かすことができない。
notes.bodyEn: A bed that uses a tree stump as its post, just as it stood. Because the room was built without cutting the root, it cannot be moved from its original place.

units.en: When she heard the sure proofs Ulysses now gave her, she fairly broke down. She flew weeping to his side, flung her arms about his neck, and kissed him. “Do not be angry with me Ulysses,” she cried, “you, who are the wisest of mankind. We have suffered, both of us. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth, and of growing old, together; do not then be aggrieved or take it amiss that I did not embrace you thus as soon as I saw you. I have been shuddering all the time through fear that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story; for there are many very wicked people going about. Jove’s daughter Helen would never have yielded herself to a man from a foreign country, if she had known that the sons of Achaeans would come after her and bring her back. Heaven put it in her heart to do wrong, and she gave no thought to that sin, which has been the source of all our sorrows. Now, however, that you have convinced me by showing that you know all about our bed (which no human being has ever seen but you and I and a single maidservant, the daughter of Actor, who was given me by my father on my marriage, and who keeps the doors of our room) hard of belief though I have been I can mistrust no longer.”
units.ja: オデュッセウスが今示した確かな証しを聞くと、彼女はとうに崩れるように泣きくずれた。彼のもとへ飛んで行き、両腕をその首に回しかけて、口づけした。「お怒りにならないでください、オデュッセウス」と彼女は叫んだ。「人間のうちで最も賢いあなた。私たちは二人とも、つらい思いをしてきました。天は、私たちが若い時代をともに過ごし、ともに老いていく幸せを許しませんでした。ですから、あなたの姿を見たそのときにすぐ抱きつかなかったからといって、心を痛めたり、とがめたりなさらないでください。私はずっと、誰かがここへ来て嘘の話で私を欺くのではないかと、恐ろしくて震えていました。世の中には、ひどく悪い者がたくさん歩き回っていますから。ゼウスの娘ヘレネも、アカイア勢の息子たちが彼女を追って来て連れ戻すと知っていたなら、よその国の男に身をゆだねたりはしなかったでしょう。天が彼女の心に悪しきことを思い起こさせ、彼女はその罪を顧みなかった。それが私たちの悲しみすべての源となったのです。けれど今は、あなたが私たちの寝台についてすべてを知っていると示して、私を納得させてくださいました——その寝台を見たのは、あなたと私、そしてただ一人の侍女、私が結婚のときに父から与えられたアクトルの娘のほかには、人間には誰もおりません。その女が私たちの部屋の扉を守っております。疑い深い私でしたが、もう疑うことはできません。」

notes.title: ヘレネ
notes.body: ゼウスとレダの娘で、スパルタの王メネラオスの妻。トロイアの王子パリスに連れ去られたことが、トロイア戦争の発端になったと語られる。
notes.bodyEn: The daughter of Zeus and Leda and the wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Her being carried off by the Trojan prince Paris is told to have been the origin of the Trojan War.

units.en: Then Ulysses in his turn melted, and wept as he clasped his dear and faithful wife to his bosom. As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves; a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger—even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck. Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.
units.ja: そこでオデュッセウスの方も心がとけて、愛する忠実な妻を胸に抱きしめて泣いた。ポセイドンが風と波の猛りで船を難破させ、泳いで岸を目指す者たちにとって陸の姿が見えるのがどれほど嬉しいか、そのうちわずかな者だけが陸にたどり着き、塩まみれの体で、堅い地面に上がり危険を脱したことをありがたく思う——そのように、妻にとって夫は、姿を見るだけでありがたいものだった。彼女は美しい二本の腕を彼の首から離せなかった。実際、二人は夜明けのバラ色の指が現れるまで悲しみにふけり続けたことだろう。だがアテナが別のことを定め、夜をはるか西に引き留め、暁の女神がオケアノスを離れることも、人々の上に夜を明けさせるために彼女を運ぶ二頭の馬ラムポスとパエトンに軛を掛けることもお許しにならなかった。

notes.title: 暁の女神エオス
notes.body: 夜明けを告げる女神で、「バラ色の指の暁」はホメロスが彼女を呼ぶ定型の言い方。馬の「パエトン」は太陽神ヘリオスの息子と同名だが、ここでは暁の女神の馬を指す。
notes.bodyEn: The goddess who announces the dawn; "rosy-fingered dawn" is Homer's formulaic way of calling her. The horse "Phaethon" shares its name with the son of the sun god Helios, but here it refers to the horse of the goddess of dawn.

units.en: At last, however, Ulysses said, “Wife, we have not yet reached the end of our troubles. I have an unknown amount of toil still to undergo. It is long and difficult, but I must go through with it, for thus the shade of Teiresias prophesied concerning me, on the day when I went down into Hades to ask about my return and that of my companions. But now let us go to bed, that we may lie down and enjoy the blessed boon of sleep.”
units.ja: やがてオデュッセウスは言った。「妻よ、私たちの苦難はまだ終わりに達してはいない。私にはまだ、どれほどのものになるかも分からない労苦が残っている。長く困難な道のりだが、やり遂げねばならない。私が冥府へ下り、自分の帰還と仲間たちのことを尋ねた日に、テイレシアスの亡霊が私についてこう予言したのだ。だが今は床につこう。横になって、眠りというありがたい恵みを味わうために。」

notes.title: テイレシアス
notes.body: テーバイの盲いた予言者。死後も冥府で知恵を保ち、オデュッセウスが冥府へ下ったとき、帰還の行く末を告げた。
notes.bodyEn: The blind prophet of Thebes. Even after death he retains wisdom in the underworld, and when Odysseus descended there, he told him how his return would end.

units.en: “You shall go to bed as soon as you please,” replied Penelope, “now that the gods have sent you home to your own good house and to your country. But as heaven has put it in your mind to speak of it, tell me about the task that lies before you. I shall have to hear about it later, so it is better that I should be told at once.”
units.ja: 「あなたがお望みのときに床につけばよろしい」とペネロペは答えた。「神々があなたを、あなた自身の立派な館へ、あなたの国へお帰しになったのですから。けれど、その話をなさるおつもりが天から与えられたのなら、あなたの前に残る務めについて話してください。いずれ聞かねばならないことですから、今すぐに聞かせていただく方がよいのです。」

units.en: “My dear,” answered Ulysses, “why should you press me to tell you? Still, I will not conceal it from you, though you will not like it. I do not like it myself, for Teiresias bade me travel far and wide, carrying an oar, till I came to a country where the people have never heard of the sea, and do not even mix salt with their food. They know nothing about ships, nor oars that are as the wings of a ship. He gave me this certain token which I will not hide from you. He said that a wayfarer should meet me and ask me whether it was a winnowing shovel that I had on my shoulder. On this, I was to fix my oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, a bull, and a boar to Neptune; after which I was to go home and offer hecatombs to all the gods in heaven, one after the other. As for myself, he said that death should come to me from the sea, and that my life should ebb away very gently when I was full of years and peace of mind, and my people should bless me. All this, he said, should surely come to pass.”
units.ja: 「妻よ」とオデュッセウスは答えた。「なぜ私に話すようせかすのだ。とはいえ、お前が快く思わないだろうと分かっていても、隠しはしない。私自身も快くは思わない。テイレシアスは、私がオールを携えて、人々が海のことを聞いたこともなく、食べ物に塩を混ぜることさえしない国へ着くまで、遠く広く旅せよと命じた。彼らは船も、船の翼のようなオールも知らない。彼は私に、隠し立てをしない確かな印を与えた。道行く人が私に出会って、肩に載せているのは唐箕かと尋ねるであろう、と言うのだ。そのとき私はオールを地面に突き立て、ポセイドンに雄羊と雄牛と雄猪をいけにえとして捧げ、そのあと家へ帰り、天のすべての神々に次々と百頭の犠牲を捧げよ、と。私自身については、死は海からやって来て、私が齢を重ね、心の安らぎに満ちたとき、私の命はごく穏やかに消えていき、民は私を祝福するだろう、と言った。これらすべては必ず実現すると彼は言った。」

notes.title: 唐箕（とうみ）
notes.body: 脱穀した穀物を風で吹き分ける農具。オールをそれと見誤る土地とは、海を知らない内陸の国のことである。
notes.bodyEn: An farming implement that separates threshed grain by blowing it with wind. The land where an oar is mistaken for one is an inland country that does not know the sea.

units.en: And Penelope said, “If the gods are going to vouchsafe you a happier time in your old age, you may hope then to have some respite from misfortune.”
units.ja: そしてペネロペは言った。「神々があなたの老年に、より幸せな時をお与えになるというのなら、そのときには不幸からしばしの息抜きが得られると思ってよいのでしょう。」

units.en: Thus did they converse. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse took torches and made the bed ready with soft coverlets; as soon as they had laid them, the nurse went back into the house to go to her rest, leaving the bed chamber woman Eurynome to show Ulysses and Penelope to bed by torch light. When she had conducted them to their room she went back, and they then came joyfully to the rites of their own old bed. Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd now left off dancing, and made the women leave off also. They then laid themselves down to sleep in the cloisters.
units.ja: こうして二人は語り合っていた。その間、エウリュノメと乳母は松明を取り、柔らかな掛け布を敷いて寝床を整えた。敷き終えると、乳母は休みに向かって家の中へ戻り、寝室づきの女エウリュノメが、松明の灯でオデュッセウスとペネロペを寝床へ案内した。エウリュノメは二人を部屋へ導くと戻っていき、二人は喜びに満ちて、かつて自分たちのものであった寝床の営みへと向かった。テレマコス、ピロイティオス、豚飼いはここで踊りをやめ、女たちにもやめさせた。そして彼らは回廊に横になって眠った。

notes.title: 「寝床の儀」という表現
notes.body: 「かつて自分たちのものであった寝床の儀」は、夫婦の床の交わりを婉曲に言い表した表現。この寝床はオデュッセウスが自ら作った寝台とされ、本巻の前半、ペネロペがその秘密を口にしたことで二人の再会が決まった、と読むことができる。
notes.titleEn: The expression "the rite of the bed"
notes.bodyEn: "The rite of the bed that once was theirs" is a euphemistic expression for the marital union of husband and wife. This bed is said to be the bedstead Odysseus made himself, and it can be read that in the first half of this book, Penelope's speaking of its secret is what settled the two's reunion.

units.en: When Ulysses and Penelope had had their fill of love they fell talking with one another. She told him how much she had had to bear in seeing the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had killed so many sheep and oxen on her account, and had drunk so many casks of wine. Ulysses in his turn told her what he had suffered, and how much trouble he had himself given to other people. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never went to sleep till he had ended his whole story.
units.ja: オデュッセウスとペネロペは愛を満たすと、互いに語り合い始めた。彼女は、自分のせいで家が悪しき求婚者の群れで満たされ、彼らが自分のためにあれほど多くの羊や牛を殺し、あれほど多くの樽の葡萄酒を飲み干したのを見て、どれほど耐え忍ばねばならなかったかを語った。オデュッセウスのほうは、自分が味わった苦しみ、そして自分が他人にどれほどの厄介をかけたかを語った。彼は何もかも語り、彼女はそれを聞くのが嬉しくて、彼が物語のすべてを終えるまで決して眠らなかった。

units.en: He began with his victory over the Cicons, and how he thence reached the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters. He told her all about the Cyclops and how he had punished him for having so ruthlessly eaten his brave comrades; how he then went on to Aeolus, who received him hospitably and furthered him on his way, but even so he was not to reach home, for to his great grief a hurricane carried him out to sea again; how he went on to the Laestrygonian city Telepylos, where the people destroyed all his ships with their crews, save himself and his own ship only. Then he told of cunning Circe and her craft, and how he sailed to the chill house of Hades, to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Teiresias, and how he saw his old comrades in arms, and his mother who bore him and brought him up when he was a child; how he then heard the wondrous singing of the Sirens, and went on to the wandering rocks and terrible Charybdis and to Scylla, whom no man had ever yet passed in safety; how his men then ate the cattle of the sun-god, and how Jove therefore struck the ship with his thunderbolts, so that all his men perished together, himself alone being left alive; how at last he reached the Ogygian island and the nymph Calypso, who kept him there in a cave, and fed him, and wanted him to marry her, in which case she intended making him immortal so that he should never grow old, but she could not persuade him to let her do so; and how after much suffering he had found his way to the Phaeacians, who had treated him as though he had been a god, and sent him back in a ship to his own country after having given him gold, bronze, and raiment in great abundance. This was the last thing about which he told her, for here a deep sleep took hold upon him and eased the burden of his sorrows.
units.ja: 彼は、キコネス人に打ち勝ったことから語り始め、そこから肥沃なロトス食い人たちの土地へたどり着いた次第を話した。キュクロプスのこと、そしてその者が彼の勇敢な仲間たちをあまりに無慈悲に食い殺したためにどれほど罰せられたかを、残らず語った。次にアイオロスのもとへ赴いたこと、アイオロスは彼を手厚くもてなして旅路を後押ししてくれたが、それでも故郷へ帰ることはかなわず、悲しみのうちに嵐が彼を再び沖へと運び去ったことを話した。さらにラエストリュゴネス人の町テレピュロスへ行ったこと、そこで人々が彼の船を乗員もろともすべて滅ぼし、彼自身と自分の船一隻だけが残ったことを語った。それから狡知に長けたキルケとその術のことを語り、ハデスの冷たい館へ航海して、テバイの預言者テイレシアスの亡霊に助言を求めたこと、かつての戦友たちや、自分を産み、幼い頃に育てた母に会ったことを話した。続いてセイレンたちの不思議な歌声を聞いたこと、漂流する岩や恐ろしいカリュブディス、そしてこれまで誰一人として無事に通り過ぎた者のいないスキュラへと進んだことを語った。次に、部下たちが太陽神の牛を食べたため、ゼウスが雷霆で船を打ち、部下たちが皆もろとも滅び、自分だけが生き残ったことを話した。最後に、オギュギアの島とニュンペーのカリュプソにたどり着いたこと、カリュプソは彼を洞窟に留めて養い、自分の夫にしたいと望み、そうすれば彼を不死の身にして決して老いさせまいとしたが、彼を説得してそうさせることはできなかったことを語った。そして多くの苦難の末にパイアケス人のもとへたどり着き、彼らは自分を神のように扱い、金や青銅、衣をふんだんに与えたうえで、船で故郷へ送り返してくれたことを話した。これが彼女に語った最後のことで、ここで深い眠りが彼をとらえ、悲しみの重荷を和らげた。

notes.title: Jove（ユピテル）とゼウス
notes.body: 原文の「Jove（ユピテル）」はローマ神話での呼び名で、ギリシアのゼウスにあたる。バトラーの英訳は神々にラテン名（Jove、Minerva、Juno など）を用いるが、本訳ではゼウス、アテナ、ヘラに統一している。
notes.bodyEn: In the original, "Jove (Jupiter)" is the name in Roman myth, corresponding to the Greek Zeus. Butler's English translation uses Latin names for the gods (Jove, Minerva, Juno, and so on), but this translation standardizes them to Zeus, Athena, and Hera.

units.en: Then Minerva bethought her of another matter. When she deemed that Ulysses had had both of his wife and of repose, she bade gold-enthroned Dawn rise out of Oceanus that she might shed light upon mankind. On this, Ulysses rose from his comfortable bed and said to Penelope, “Wife, we have both of us had our full share of troubles, you, here, in lamenting my absence, and I in being prevented from getting home though I was longing all the time to do so. Now, however, that we have at last come together, take care of the property that is in the house. As for the sheep and goats which the wicked suitors have eaten, I will take many myself by force from other people, and will compel the Achaeans to make good the rest till they shall have filled all my yards. I am now going to the wooded lands out in the country to see my father who has so long been grieved on my account, and to yourself I will give these instructions, though you have little need of them. At sunrise it will at once get abroad that I have been killing the suitors; go upstairs, therefore, and stay there with your women. See nobody and ask no questions.”
units.ja: そこでアテナは別のことを思いめぐらせた。オデュッセウスが妻と休息の両方を十分に得たと見て取ると、彼女は黄金の玉座に坐す暁の女神に、オケアノスから昇って人々に光を注ぐよう命じた。そこでオデュッセウスは心地よい寝床から起き上がり、ペネロペに言った。「妻よ、われら二人はいずれも苦難を十分に分け持った。お前はここで私の不在を嘆くことによって、私は、帰りたいと願い続けながら故郷へ帰ることを妨げられることによって。だが今や、われらはついに再びいっしょになったのだから、家の中にある財産をよく守るがよい。悪しき求婚者たちが食らった羊や山羊については、私自身が他の者たちから力ずくで多くを奪い取り、残りはアカイア勢に弁償させて、私の家畜囲いをすべて満たさせよう。私はこれから、私のために長く悲しんできた父に会うために、田舎の森の地へ行く。お前にはこの指示を与えておくが、お前はそれをほとんど必要としていない。日が昇れば、私が求婚者たちを殺したことがすぐに広まるだろう。だから二階へ上がり、女たちとともにそこに留まりなさい。誰にも会わず、何も尋ねてはならない。」

notes.title: 暁の女神エオス
notes.body: 「黄金の玉座に坐す暁」は暁の女神エオス。毎朝オケアノスの流れから昇り、人々に光をもたらすとされる。
notes.bodyEn: "Dawn seated on her golden throne" is Eos, the goddess of dawn. Each morning she rises from the stream of Ocean and is said to bring light to people.

units.en: As he spoke he girded on his armour. Then he roused Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus, and told them all to put on their armour also. This they did, and armed themselves. When they had done so, they opened the gates and sallied forth, Ulysses leading the way. It was now daylight, but Minerva nevertheless concealed them in darkness and led them quickly out of the town.
units.ja: こう言いながら、彼は武具を身に着けた。それからテレマコス、ピロイティオス、エウマイオスを呼び起こし、彼らにも皆、武具を着けるよう命じた。彼らはそのとおりにして武装した。そうし終えると、彼らは門を開けて打って出た。オデュッセウスが先頭に立った。すでに夜は明けていたが、それでもアテナは彼らを闇で包み隠し、すばやく町の外へと導き出した。
